prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat electronic bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is a verified discovery with a clear physical core: a continuum-model prediction (Bistritzer and MacDonald, 2011) that a small twist quenches the bandwidth, followed in 2018 by the observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity in exactly that regime. Theory told experimenters where to look and experiment confirmed it, which is the tie between calculation and measurement that I value most. Since 2018 the correlated phases have been reproduced by many independent groups using transport, scanning probes and spectroscopy, and the field has grown into tunable moire quantum matter, including topological and fractional Chern states. It also echoes the 2010 graphene prize: a material that theorists did not expect to behave this way gave a new platform for quantum behaviour. Having reread the ballots, I still rank it first, and I note that it is the only shortlisted entry in which my own subfield can judge both the prediction and the confirmation directly.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is maturity of interpretation. The pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is unresolved, twist-angle disorder makes sample-to-sample details irreproducible, and the field is only eight years old, so a prize now may be judged early compared with optical lattice clocks (B024) or lattice quantum simulation (B020), which have two decades of independent confirmation. There is also an allocation problem: Cao and other first experimental authors, and parallel experimental groups, are not creditable within the supplied names, and the three-person limit forces a choice that will look incomplete.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B021 fourth and would favour the pair MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, leaving out Bistritzer because of the three-person limit, while noting that Cao as first experimental author cannot be represented.
responses.response: I take the point about Cao seriously, and I agree that the experimental credit is not fully representable. But I would keep Bistritzer. The 2011 magic-angle prediction is a two-author result, and a prize that names only MacDonald would credit the prediction to the senior author alone and misstate who found the flat-band mechanism. The theory slot is the one place where the supplied names do match the history, so the cost of dropping him is higher than the gain of a tidier pair. I would accept the pair as a fallback if colleagues think three names overstate the case, but I do not see it as the better configuration.

responses.point: Kroll puts optical lattice clocks (B024) first because it is a measurement that changes what can be measured, is reproduced by several national laboratories, and has a pending redefinition of the second.
responses.response: This is the strongest competing case on maturity, and I rank it seventh mainly because I know less about the field, not because the work is weak. I share your view that independent confirmation across JILA, RIKEN, PTB and SYRTE is excellent. My qualification is that the lattice clock is an improvement of a precision-measurement technique in a line already honoured in 2005 for the comb and in 2012 for ion control, whereas the twisted-bilayer case reveals new phases of matter. I would hold B024 as my first alternative. Whether the committee prefers instrument-driven progress to a discovery about nature is a genuine difference in values, and I do not think either view is wrong.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks quantum simulation with ultracold atoms in optical lattices (B020) first, arguing that Hubbard and Mott physics became controllable and observable, with single-site resolution and broad reach.
responses.response: I agree that B020 is mature and well confirmed, and as a theorist of correlated electrons I welcome the benchmarks it gives for DFT+DMFT-type methods. My concern is that it is a diffuse discovery with five credited names, and any trio leaves out Esslinger or Cirac or Zoller, so the credit would be contested whichever choice is made. It also overlaps with the 2001 condensate prize and the 2012 and 2022 quantum prizes. I also have not seen yet that lattice simulation has answered an open question of correlated-electron theory, for example the doped Hubbard model. I would keep it as an alternative but not as the preferred configuration.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks Dynamical mean-field theory (B019) third and the twisted bilayer graphene prize sixth, arguing that the unsettled interpretation of superconductivity argues for waiting.
responses.response: We agree on B019 as scientifically strong, and I ranked it third myself. On twisted bilayer graphene, I accept that the pairing mechanism is open, but the central discovery, correlated insulators and superconductivity in flat bands, is not in dispute and has been confirmed by many groups. A prize does not have to wait for the mechanism of the superconductivity to be settled, any more than the 1987 prize for high-temperature superconductivity did. My reservation about B019 is the opposite one: it is a method, and the omission of Metzner and Muller-Hartmann is a real attribution problem that does not apply to B021.

responses.point: Olsson ranks room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance (B005) first for an unambiguous experimental discovery that became a core device effect, and puts twisted bilayer graphene second with a note that recognition is slightly early.
responses.response: I ranked B005 fourth and share your respect for it; the first-principles prediction of coherent MgO tunnelling is a good example of theory preceding experiment. My difficulty is the attribution that you also flag: Yuasa and Djayaprawira, and the theorists Butler and Mathon, sit outside the credited names, and the effect is a continuation of the spin-electronics line honoured in 2007. On your remark that B021 may be slightly early, I think eight years of broad replication is enough for the central result, though I accept that a later year would reduce the risk. I would be willing to discuss B005 for the future, but not as a combination with B021 because the three-person limit does not allow it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee is comfortable awarding a field whose superconducting pairing mechanism is still unresolved, or would prefer to wait.
Whether a three-name credit (MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer) is more defensible than the pair, given that Cao and others cannot be named.
Whether a two-part prize combining B021 with a second achievement is possible within the three-person limit; I could not construct a satisfactory one from the supplied names.
How much weight the committee gives to the age of the optical lattice clock and quantum simulation fields against the youth of moire physics.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile: I have no recorded connection to MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer or the other shortlisted candidates. My field (DFT, magnetism) is close to B019 and B005, which I treat as scientific proximity, not a conflict.
